prompt.context: Our client is Rotisserie Ranch, a poultry farming company that specializes in growing chickens for rotisserie roasting. Its primary customer segment is comprised of large grocery chains that buy its chickens to fresh roast in the meat departments of their grocery stores. Market research has revealed to Rotisserie Ranch that more and more consumers have begun buying flavored rotisserie chickens recently.
prompt.question: Rotisserie Ranch is thinking of pre-flavoring some of its chickens for grocers. What would you consider in making this recommendation?

clarifying_info.q: Is there competition in the pre-seasoned chicken space?
clarifying_info.a: For the purposes of this case, assume Rotisserie Ranch will only compete against existing Private Label brands at grocery stores. Competitors freeze their chickens, so they cannot pre-season them.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have any competitive advantage enabling this?
clarifying_info.a: The client has a patented process for sterilely packaging chicken so that it remains fresh for 30 days, making freezing unnecessary.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's current market position?
clarifying_info.a: The client is currently the industry market share leader in rotisserie-ready chicken.

clarifying_info.q: How many and which flavors are being considered?
clarifying_info.a: Four new flavored products to be introduced concurrently: Barbecue, lemon herb, tandoori, and teriyaki.

clarifying_info.q: What happens to unsold cooked chickens?
clarifying_info.a: Predicting demand for cooked chickens is difficult for grocers; any leftover cooked chickens at the end of the day are thrown out. Unthawed chickens cannot be re-frozen.

exhibits.title: Store sales
exhibits.shows: A table comparing weekly sales data for Standard Rotisserie chicken (Stores A and B) versus BBQ Seasoned Rotisserie chicken (Stores C and D), including retail price and retailer margin for each store.

framework: Value to customers (grocery chains): Will grocers want to buy pre-seasoned chicken?
Revenue and cost implications: Does the cost increase to client get offset by a price increase to grocers?
Competition: Who else offers pre-seasoned rotisserie chicken and what is the competitive dynamic?
Market testing: How do we validate demand before a full rollout?

questions.prompt: Prompt 1: Do you think that grocery retailers would be interested in pre-seasoned chickens from Rotisserie Ranch?
questions.guidance: There is no single correct answer; evaluate the quality of reasoning. A strong 'Yes' argument covers: (1) Labor cost reduction — meat department workers no longer need to season chickens; (2) Economies of scale — centralized seasoning lowers cost per unit; (3) Product consistency — centrally managed R&D produces more consistent flavor profiles. A strong 'No' argument covers: (1) Loss of differentiation — grocery chains differentiate on value-added services; (2) Local taste preferences — grocers may be better at gauging local consumer tastes; (3) Inventory complexity — more SKUs increases inventory management burden.

questions.prompt: Prompt 2: After several interviews, grocers are very interested in the proposed new product, but first they want to be sure the chickens will sell well. How would you make sure?
questions.guidance: The correct answer is to run a test market for the new products. A strong candidate will identify: (1) A pilot/market test should be run; (2) The pilot needs a control or comparison group to isolate the effect of the pre-seasoning. The interviewer should cut off further elaboration once the candidate demonstrates understanding of these two points.

questions.prompt: Prompt 3: A test market launch for the new Rotisserie Ranch BBQ chicken was administered. Using Exhibit 1, what is the overall profit for both Store A and B (standard) and for both Store C and D (BBQ seasoned) from the test market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate retailer profit for standard chicken versus BBQ seasoned chicken and compare totals. Retailer profit = weekly sales * retailer margin. The BBQ seasoned stores generate $175 more in combined weekly retailer profit than the standard stores.

math.setup: Retailer profit = weekly sales * retailer margin. Compare combined profit of standard chicken stores (A+B) to BBQ seasoned stores (C+D).
steps: Difference: $1,075 - $900 = $175/week more profit for grocers with BBQ seasoned chicken
math.answer: Standard rotisserie total retailer profit = $900/week; BBQ seasoned rotisserie total retailer profit = $1,075/week; BBQ seasoned generates $175 more per week in retailer profit.

recommendation: Rotisserie Ranch should launch the pre-seasoned BBQ chicken product and test the remaining three flavors (lemon herb, tandoori, teriyaki).

Consumers are shifting toward seasoned rotisserie chicken, and the test market confirms grocers earn more profit ($175/week incremental) with the BBQ seasoned product versus standard rotisserie chicken.
The client's patented sterile packaging process provides a defensible competitive moat — no competitor can replicate the pre-seasoned fresh chicken offering.
risks: Test market results may not be representative of all markets or all four flavors.
Demand forecasting for cooked/perishable chicken remains difficult; unsold inventory is written off at end of day.
Introducing four flavors simultaneously increases SKU complexity and inventory risk at grocery stores.
Retailer margin drops from 30% to 25% on the new product, which may create pricing negotiation friction over time.
next_steps: Conduct broader market tests for the remaining three flavors (lemon herb, tandoori, teriyaki) using a similar control/test store methodology.
Analyze client-side cost implications of pre-seasoning to confirm overall profitability improvement for Rotisserie Ranch, not just for grocers.
Develop demand forecasting tools with grocery partners to minimize end-of-day waste for the perishable pre-seasoned product.
Formalize go-to-market plan for national rollout based on expanded test market results.
